Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
revision_notes: Original ITU LDC country-profile citation (2017 PDF) is dead/inaccessible, and its cited figure of ~76 kbit/s per user in the Comments field is inconsistent with the assigned Value Code of 1 (Very Low, <5 kbit/s), so the original row could not be confirmed as recorded. The World Bank's 2021/22 Digital Economy for Africa diagnostic for Sudan (published 2023) reports used international bandwidth of 245 Mbps against a population of 42.8 million in 2019, equivalent to 5.7 kbit/s per capita; since internet users are a subset of total population (around 26% of Sudanese used the internet in 2019, per World Bank WDI), bandwidth per internet user would be materially higher than this population-wide floor, plausibly in the high-teens to low-twenties kbit/s range - i.e. Low to Moderate on the scale, not Very Low. This is a derived estimate combining two indicators rather than a single directly-reported 'per internet user' ITU figure, and it pre-dates the civil war that broke out in April 2023, which has severely disrupted network operations (power cuts, infrastructure damage, service blackouts) even though the Port Sudan submarine cable landings remain physically intact. Given this compounded uncertainty, a conservative recalculation to code 2 (Low, 5-19 kbit/s) is proposed rather than the higher point estimate, and the row is flagged for human review to confirm with a current, directly-sourced figure if one becomes available.
revised_comments: Sudan's international internet bandwidth is difficult to pin down precisely on a per-internet-user basis. World Bank data for 2019 put used international bandwidth at 245 Mbps against a population of 42.8 million (5.7 kbit/s per capita), and with roughly 26% internet penetration that year, bandwidth per internet user is estimated in the high-teens to low-twenties kbit/s range - placing capacity in the low band rather than the very low band. Four submarine cable systems land at Port Sudan (EASSy, FALCON, SAS-1, SAS-2), giving reasonable first-mile capacity, but the civil war since April 2023 has caused widespread network disruption through infrastructure damage, power outages and enforced blackouts, so actual current per-user bandwidth is likely lower than this pre-war estimate and remains unconfirmed.
